figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Phase transition under a sloppy oracle. We vary a single noise knob J, defined as J = 1 − δFP − δFN = TPR − FPR, which summarizes the net effect of false-positive and false-negative reward corruption induced by a noisy oracle. As J crosses zero, we observe a sharp transition from Phase I (learning; J > 0, accuracy improves with training and the bad-solution mass p for a prompt converges to 0) to Phase II (unlearning; J < 0, accuracy systematically degrades and p converges to 1), with J = 0 as the critical boundary. Curves report validation performance during GRPO training on a Python code-generation task (two epochs) starting from Qwen-2.5-3B; solid lines denote the run-averaged E[pass@1] and shaded bands indicate 95% confidence intervals across runs. Although our mean-field ODE characterizes the training-time dynamics of p, the same sign-of-J transition is mirrored on held-out validation prompts in this setup, suggesting the drift is not merely a training-set artifact.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: The Winner Takes It All. The GRPO mean-field dynamics exhibit a striking structural property: in the absence of any symmetry among initial good arm masses, one arm ultimately dominates. When the oracle is in the learning regime (J = TPR − FPR > 0), the total bad-arm mass p(t) converges to 0, and among the good arms the algorithm converges to the one with the highest initial probability (see Appendix I for a rigorous theoretical analysis of this phenomenon.). At the critical boundary (J = 0), the probability vector remains fixed throughout training, yielding a continuum of equilibrium points. In the unlearning regime (J < 0), the flow reverses and the bad arm becomes the almost-sure winner. This “winner-take-all” behavior is an inherent feature of the GRPO-style replicator dynamics.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Rate, not Fate. Our mean-field multi-armed bandit analysis predicts that, whenever learning succeeds (J > 0), training with noisy rewards asymptotically converges to the same final accuracy as training on clean rewards; the noise level controls only the convergence speed, not the eventual performance. The same phenomena happen for J < 0. Our mean field model, along with experimental observation in Fig. 1 supports the “convergence rate is different, fate is the same” prediction.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Geometry of the Probability Simplex. The policy p evolves on the non-Euclidean manifold ∆K+M−1. The softmax Jacobian J(p) endows this space with the Shahshahani (Fisher) geometry, projecting updates onto the zero-sum tangent space Tp. GRPO induces a mass-conserving replicator flow, ṗ = ηJ(p)A, which dynamically redistributes probability mass based on relative advantage. In the local tangent space, the forward KL divergence manifests as the quadratic form 1/2δ⊤Diag(p)−1δ, identifying J(p) as the inverse Riemannian metric.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: KL regularization smooths the phase transition at J = 0 via an interior fixed point. Incorporating a KL penalty toward a reference mass pref introduces a restoring drift, resulting in the regularized ODE equation 18. For any β > 0, the system possesses a unique stable interior equilibrium p⋆ ∈ (0,1) defined by the balance condition equation 19. This equilibrium satisfies p⋆ < pref for J > 0, p⋆ = pref at J = 0, and p⋆ > pref for J < 0. The reward-driven component is modulated by the multi-block collision factor C(y,z) = ∥y∥2 2 + ∥z∥2 2 ∈ [1/K + 1/M,2]. As β → ∞, the equilibrium approaches pref due to strong anchoring; as β ↓ 0, it approaches the reward-driven boundary, effectively smoothing the boundary collapse into a controlled interior state.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Reward-variance geometry under noisy Bernoulli rewards. (Left) Reward variance Var(r) = q(p) (1 − q(p)) as a function of bad mass p for representative noise settings; markers indicate p⋆ = argmaxp∈[0,1] Var(r) (equivalently q(p) = 1/2 when attainable, otherwise the boundary p ∈ {0,1}). (Middle) Heatmap of p⋆(δFN,δFP) in the informative region J > 0, with the dashed diagonal marking the phase boundary J = 1 − δFN − δFP = 0 and contours showing level sets of p⋆. (Right) Maximum achievable reward standard deviation σmax(δFN,δFP) = maxp∈[0,1] sqrt(q(p)(1 − q(p))) with contours. Throughout, q(p) = (1 − δFN) − Jp and J = 1 − δFN − δFP.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7: Learnability-maximizing bad mass p† under group z-scored rewards. We plot the instantaneous learnability speed L(p) = J/σ(p) [p(1 − p)]2, which controls the magnitude of the one-step bad-mass drift |∆p| ∝ L(p) (up to a positive constant), where σ(p) = sqrt(q(p)(1 − q(p))), q(p) = (1 − δFN) − Jp, and J = 1 − δFN − δFP. (A) Curves of L(p) versus p for representative noise settings; markers indicate p† = argmaxp∈[0,1] L(p). (B) Heatmap of p†(δFN,δFP) in the informative region J > 0 (masked for J ≤ 0); the dashed diagonal marks J = 0 and contours indicate level sets of p†. (C) Heatmap of the maximum instantaneous learnability maxp L(p), showing how noise reduces the peak achievable drift. Symmetric noise (δFN = δFP) preserves the midpoint optimum p† = 1/2, while asymmetric noise shifts the maximizer away from 1/2 by reweighting the signal through σ(p)−1.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: The unnumbered title graphic establishes rate/fate; Figure 1 measures the J phase boundary; Figure 2 turns the sign into simplex phases; Figure 3 separates rate from fate; Figure 4 supplies geometry; Figure 5 supplies KL intervention; Table 1 closes the main experiment; Appendix Figures 6–7 diagnose variance/learnability and Tables 2–4 close stability and reproduction.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Figures 1–7 use a bold short headline followed by setup, encoding/comparison or mechanism, and a stated interpretation; Figures 1, 6 and 7 define uncertainty/contours/abbreviations, while Figures 2, 3 and 5 use theory/appendix pointers. Table 1 explains its gain/loss bars; Tables 2–4 use concise functional captions.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Table 1 uses J, error rates, pass@1, relative improvement and a bar column; Tables 2–3 share equilibrium/condition/stability; Table 4 uses lifecycle section headers with key/value columns. Horizontal rules and absent vertical rules keep appendix tables in one booktabs/minimal family.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Eqs. (1)–(6) and Theorem 6.1 define J → advantage gap → bad-mass drift, which Figure 1 and Table 1 test under controlled noise. Figures 2–5 are theory/mechanism, Figures 6–7 are analytic diagnostics, and the two J=0.3 rows in Table 1 are the only explicit within-J comparison; no empirical β/G/model/task/clipping ablation is present.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Figure 2 points to Appendix I; Figures 5–7 align with Appendices G, B and D; Tables 2–3 align with I/J; Table 4 aligns with L; Algorithm 1 and the kMarsh sample align with M/N. Appendix A–H provide the formal bandit, noise, ODE, learnability, Lyapunov, clipping, KL and geometry foundations.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: PDF body, captions and booktabs tables primarily use URW Palladio plus Computer Modern/Pazo math objects. The title graphic and raster assets introduce SketchBlock/Myriad/emoji display roles, so the page-level typography is intentionally mixed and the editable font provenance of most source assets is unavailable.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: J sign is a recurring blue/gold/red semantic spine across Figures 1–3 and 5–7; geometry adds orange/blue/purple, and Tables 1–4 remain black/white. Direct labels, markers, contours and rules provide limited redundancy, but colorbars, masks and many phase distinctions are not grayscale-safe.

most_reusable_patterns: Carry one interpretable scalar (J) through curve color, phase portrait, ODE field and diagnostic heatmaps, and define its direction in the caption.
Use a main trajectory chart with same-hue uncertainty bands and direct phase labels, then provide exact conditions and baseline deltas in a compact table.

For theory, pair parameter–time fields with representative trajectories; for related analytic objectives, reuse a curve + argmax heatmap + maximum heatmap triptych; keep mirrored stability tables on the same header grammar.
highest_value_objects: Figure 1 + Table 1 for the finite-horizon H1 result
failure_patterns: The title graphic is decorative and symbol-dense, and several wide composites use small labels, many colorbars or formula annotations.
Figures 6–7 have exact embedded raster assets but no public replotting generator; most other figures have only semantic/current rendered variants rather than the paper TeX source.
Table 1 reports point values without the run dispersion described in §7.2; the experiment has no β intervention, cross-task/model verifier validation or direct asymptotic H2 measurement.
Color-dependent masks, phase hues and continuous colorbars reduce grayscale accessibility and make later editing difficult.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: Use the positive/zero/negative J sign as a single visual spine from the title teaser and phase line chart through simplex/ODE geometry and appendix variance/learnability triptychs, then close with black-and-white stability/configuration tables while recording the partial-source and color/small-label limits.
